paper_title: TinyAstral: Transferring Self-Evolving Harnesses to Tiny Generalist Manipulation Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Robot agents built on vision-language models depend on both the planner and its harness: the tools, feedback, memory, and recovery logic around it. Can improvements to a large teacher's harness be carried into a compact agent with lower inference compute cost? We present TinyAstral, a two-stage approach. We first freeze an open-weight teacher and improve its harness through recursive self-improvement (RSI): frontier LLM agents read the teacher's trajectories and propose harness edits, and each edit is accepted only if it passes a paired statistical test. We then freeze the final harness, collect teacher trajectories with reasoning and failure recovery, and distill a small student that replaces the teacher in the same harness. On RoboTwin, harness evolution raises the teacher's success from 33.4% to 63.6%; the final 4B student reaches 62.8%. Across four harness versions, distilled 4B students score close to their corresponding teachers, and later versions yield stronger students, showing that harness evolution gains carry into compact models. The harness gains also transfer to other frozen planners without retraining. On identical episodes, the final 4B student outperforms open 4B agents, the open 27B harness-RSI model SenseNova-RoboRSI, and our own teacher model placed in three competitors' harnesses. It stays close to its teacher on all three training benchmarks, and on three benchmarks never used for RSI or training it scores close to a 552B planner running the same harness. On the measured deployment episodes, it uses about one fifth of its teacher's accelerator time.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Robot agents built on visionlanguage models depend on both the planner and its harness: the tools, feedback, memory, and recovery logic around it. Can improvements to large teachers harness be carried into compact agent with lower inference compute cost? We present TinyAstral, two-stage approach. We first freeze an open-weight teacher and improve its harness through recursive selfimprovement (RSI): frontier LLM agents read the teachers trajectories and propose harness edits, and each edit is accepted only if it passes paired statistical test. We then freeze the final harness, collect teacher trajectories with reasoning and failure recovery, and distill small student that replaces the teacher in the same harness. On RoboTwin, harness evolution raises the teachers success from 33.4% to 63.6%; the final 4B student reaches 62.8%. 1 1. Introduction Visionlanguage models (VLMs) can operate robot arms by reading images and calling perception and motion tools [11, 12, 18, 25]. The model chooses the object, action sequence, and stopping point; the surrounding harness grounds these choices, executes them, and reports what happened. Tool interfaces, feedback, task memory, and failure recovery therefore contribute to the agents performance alongside the model itself [10, 40, 46, 57]. Two lines of work offer complementary ways to build these agents. Harness evolution improves the system around frozen planner [10, 40, 46]; agent distillation trains compact models from stronger agents trajectories [24, 27, 56]. We connect these approaches by asking: can we first improve large teachers harness, then transfer the resulting decision-making capability to small model? This would allow the improved system to run with substantially less inference compute. We present TinyAstral, family of 0.8B4B manipulation agents built in two stages  (Fig. 2)  . First, we freeze the weights of an open-weight teacher, Qwen3.8-FlashNext [34], and improve its harness through master-guided recursive self-improvement (RSI) loop. Humans specify the rules and budget in advance. Frontier LLM agents then inspect failures and propose harness edits, which the system automatically accepts or rejects according to pre-registered paired statistical tests. Second, we freeze the final harness and collect teacher trajectories containing reasoning, tool calls, and recovery from injected failures. Together with auxiliary offline real-robot supervision, these trajectories train compact student to interpret feedback, choose actions, recover from failure, and decide when to finish. At deployment, the student replaces the teacher in the same frozen harness. We evaluate both stages and the connection between them. Harness evolution raises the frozen teachers RoboTwin success from 33.4% to 63.6%, and distillation produces 4B student at 62.8%. To test whether this connection holds beyond the final endpoint, we distill students at four harness versions. The four students score 36.2%, 49.8%, 60.0%, and 62.8%, each close to its corresponding teacher. The same evolved harness also improves DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and the untrained 4B initialization, showing that its gains are reusable across planners. On identical episodes the student outperforms every open competitor we ran, including our own teacher model inside three competitors harnesses (93.6% vs. 78.9% on Guava; 78.3% vs. 57.3% and 53.0% on LIBERO-PRO), and on unseen benchmarks the small 4B student scores close to 552B planner in the same harness. Our contributions are: Harness evolution followed by distillation. two-stage approach first improves frozen teachers manipulation harness, then trains compact planner from that teachers reasoning and recovery trajectories for deployment in the same harness. Evidence that evolution gains transfer. The harness improves other frozen planners, and distilled students at four harness versions track the performance of their corresponding teachers, showing that system improvements carry into compact models. Compact agents with lower inference compute cost. single TinyAstral-4B model covers six benchmarks: on identical episodes it outperforms every open competitor we ran, including our own teacher model inside three competitors harnesses, scores close to its teacher on the three training benchmarks and close to 552B planner on unseen ones, and uses about one fifth of the teachers accelerator time per episode in our deployment measurement. 2. Related Work Large models operating robots through harness. Language and vision-language models can operate robots by writing code or issuing tool calls over perception and motion primitives [11, 12, 18, 25], with spatial-reasoning models supplying grounding [32, 50]. Recent work shows that the harness around the model, namely its tool interis firstface, feedback, memory, and recovery logic, order factor. Harness VLA [57] composes frozen VLA with memory-guided agents, RoboDawn [14] and MotorMind [22] expose closed-loop interfaces to general VLM, and PyRUA-Lean [37] cuts token cost with interactive code execution. growing line also evolves the harness from execution traces: PhysEvo [40] runs recursive self-improvement around single frozen model, HarnessPAI [46] evolves an executable program, ASPIRE [28] accumulates skill library, and the two RoboRSI systems [10, 47] refine skills and agent components with validation before release. Concurrent with our work, SenseNovaRoboRSI [10] also trains 27B VLM on validated interaction experience, and World Action Agent [56] distills the tool-call traces of its skill-evolved harness into 9B VLM. We share the view that the harness is what improves while model weights stay fixed. TinyAstral differs in three ways: the harness of locally hosted open-weight teacher evolves continually under paired statistical selection, its gains are measured across planners at successive snapshots, and the evolved teacher is distilled into 0.8B, 2B, and 4B students that stay close to it. Small manipulation agents and VLAs. End-to-end VLAs such as OpenVLA [21], π0 [3], and π0.5 [31] map observations directly to actions and are trained on large robot datasets, which makes them compact at inference but dependent on in-distribution demonstrations; benchmarks 2 such as LIBERO-PRO [58] and RoboTwin 2.0 [8] probe how far they carry under perturbation. second route trains small model to be the agent instead. Guava [27] designs manipulation harness and distills reasoning and recovery trajectories from frontier VLM into 4B open model, PyRUA-Lean [37] trains 4B coder with GRPO on 45 LIBERO-PRO instances, and Robo-Harness K1 [24] and World Action Agent [56] fine-tune small VLM students on harness traces. TinyAstral first evolves the teacher harness and then freezes it for data collection and distillation. Distillation at several frozen snapshots tests whether the preceding harness improvements carry into student performance. Self-improving agents and agent distillation. Language agents can improve through stored experience and reflection [36, 44], and recent systems let model rewrite its own scaffold or code: STOP [52], ADAS [17], Godel Agent [49], and the Darwin Godel Machine [54], following the classical notion of recursive self-improvement [13]; GEPA [2] reflects on execution traces to evolve prompts. ADAS also reports transfer of discovered agents across models and domains. TinyAstral evolves the tools, execution feedback, task memory, and recovery logic of manipulation harness under paired statistical selection, and carries the evolved system into tiny student. Knowledge distillation [15, 35] and its agent variants, FireAct [6] and AgentTuning [53], transfer trajectories from strong language agent to smaller one on text and tool-use tasks; Distilling Step-by-Step [16] uses teacher rationales as extra supervision, and BetterTogether [38] alternates prompt optimization with fine-tuning of the same model. We supervise rationales together with tool calls inside closed-loop visual interaction history, and distill from teacher whose harness has already been evolved, into student of different size. 3. Method In the first, master TinyAstral has two stages  (Fig. 2)  . improves the harness of frozen teacher through statistically gated loop (Sec. 3.2). Once evolution ends, we freeze the final harness, collect teacher trajectories through it, and distill the resulting reasoning and recovery behavior into compact student (Sec. 3.3). At deployment, the student replaces the teacher in the same harness. We first define the agent and its interface (Sec. 3.1). 3.1. Planner, harness, and scoring Agent and harness. planner model π controls robot through harness H. At turn the harness gives π an observation ot, and π produces reasoning trace followed by exactly one tool call at. The harness executes the call and returns structured result rt. The harness determines how an action is carried out: perception (SAM 3 segmentation [5] lifted to depth point clouds), grasp and placement geometry, collision-free motion planning, and closed-loop corrections. The planner determines what to do: which object, which part of it, which reference and spatial relation, which arm, in what order, and when the task is finished. The model never outputs joint angles or coordinates unless tool explicitly requests them. Observations combine camera images, the task instruction, recent tool results, and gripper state. Object-level tools provide grasping, placement, verification, and recovery primitives; the full interface is specified in Sec. G. Autonomous termination and scoring. The agent ends an episode itself by calling done with the predicates it believes hold (e.g. on(a,b), upright(a), lifted(a,cm)). The harness checks these predicates with the cameras and gripper sensors; if check fails, it rejects the call and returns the measurement so the agent can keep working. After two rejections, the next done ends the episode without check. An episode also ends if the agent calls give up or exhausts its budget (30 tool calls on RoboTwin; per-benchmark limits in Sec. B). The environments success flag never enters the models input. Our primary metric, strict success S, counts an episode only if the agent ended it with done and the benchmarks success predicate holds in the final state. We also report ever success, which counts an episode if the task was achieved after any tool call. 3.2. Stage 1: Evolving the teacher harness The self-improving system consists of the frozen teacher πT , the harness H, and the master . Only changes. The weights of πT stay fixed throughout, and does not act in the environment. Humans specify the rules (including the pre-registered acceptance criteria) and budget before the loop begins. The master is set of frontier LLM agents that read trajectories, propose edits, implement them, and audit one anothers code. The system applies the pre-registered paired statistical tests to determine acceptance. Each round runs the current teacher, analyzes its failures, proposes edits, and tests candidate against the current harness. 1. Read trajectories. The current accepted harness Hk is run on development seeds. The master inspects the logged images, tool calls, tool results, and teacher reasoning, and assigns each failure to one of ten failure classes, such as off-target placement, false completion (done accepted but the final state fails), missing primitives, task-memory errors, and instance misidentification. 2. Propose edits. For target cluster of failing tasks, the master writes candidate components: new tools or primitives, more honest tool returns, perception fixes, failure han3 Figure 2. Overview of TinyAstral. Stage 1: humans specify the rules and budget in advance. master of frontier LLM agents reads trajectories of the frozen teacher acting through the harness (tools, feedback, memory, recovery) and proposes harness edits, which are accepted only if paired A/B test on selection seeds passes pre-registered statistical gate; model weights never change. Stage 2: after evolution ends, we freeze and collect teacher trajectories, including reasoning and recovery branches. These are mixed with offline real-robot supervision to train tiny students (0.8B4B), which replace the teacher in the same harness. Evaluation covers three training domains and three unseen benchmarks, plus three closed-loop real-robot tasks on an SO-ARM101 arm. dling, or local corrections to the task memory. Edits must be general. Code may not branch on the task name. In the final integration phase, the system prompt and existing tool descriptions must remain byte-identical to the parent. Memory may change only for the targeted tasks. In addition, every new component must fire through an explicit trigger that writes component-specific marker to the log. separate code audit verifies that, whenever the trigger does not fire, the candidate behaves step-for-step like the parent. 3. Test and accept edits. Candidates are compared with the current harness on the same task/seed pairs. Training, selection, and evaluation seeds occupy disjoint ranges. The pre-registered gate requires positive evidence of improvement on targeted or triggered pairs and checks for regressions elsewhere; unsuccessful candidates are rejected or stopped early. The final integration phase accepted three of seven candidates. Evaluation seeds are excluded from acceptance tests. The acceptance rules and capability ledger are in Sec. E. ones, use no task memory. From evolution to frozen teacher system. We number accepted main-line snapshots chronologically from the starting harness H0; the lineage proceeds through H16 to the final (Tab. 8). These accepted versions are distinct from the 296 candidate capabilities and the seven integration cycles in the final phase. We freeze before collecting the final teacher trajectories for distillation. 3.3. Stage 2: Collecting supervision from the frozen system The teacher πT collects trajectories through the frozen . These trajectories supervise student πS to reason about observations and feedback and choose the next tool call. The teacher weights and harness remain fixed during data collection and student training. The distillation recipe combines reasoning targets, recovery branches, strict-success filtering, and training samples exported from the exact harness interactions. Task memory. RoboTwin instructions often leave the success condition implicit (e.g. lift requires holding the object at least 10 cm up). For RoboTwin only, the harness therefore reads one short end-state note per task; the notes contain no actions or trajectories, are refined during RSI on development seeds, and are frozen and read-only at evaluation. The other five benchmarks, including all zero-shot Keep the teachers reasoning. Each training target supervises the teachers stated rationale together with its next tool call, i.e. <think>. . .</think> and then the call. Emptying the reasoning text while keeping all samples identical lowers success by 19.3 pp on LIBEROPRO, 11.2 pp on SimplerEnv Google VM, and 10.0 pp on VLABench (Sec. 4.4). 4 Recovery branches. Successful episodes rarely show how to recover from failure, so we add recovery branches. Starting from successful teacher episode, we replay its first calls in fresh simulator with the same seed, using the recorded results and without querying the model. At the branch point we inject perturbation: on RoboTwin, the grasped object slips, or the target object is moved by 610 cm before the next grasp; on Guava and LIBERO, grasp misses, push falls short, or placed object is displaced. The teacher then continues online. branch is kept only if the perturbation took effect, the replay reproduced every recorded result code, and the teacher still reached strict success. Its samples begin at the first decision after the perturbation. On RoboTwin, branches are subsampled to 20% of the RoboTwin samples (3,471 branch and 13,857 main-episode samples). Strict successes only. Main episodes run at temperature 0, as in evaluation. training seed on which the teacher fails is retried up to twice at temperature 0.7 with an unchanged prompt. We keep only episodes that the teacher ended with done and that the benchmark judges successful in the final state. Episodes that succeeded at some point but were later undone are discarded. Success labels are used offline for this selection and never appear in the training messages. Offline real-robot supervision. To expose the student to real images, we add offline data from public realrobot datasets (AgiBot World [1]; Fractal [4], BridgeData V2 [43], DROID [19], and Berkeley UR5 [7] from Open X-Embodiment [29]), cast as three auxiliary tasks in the harness format: state and failure judgment (27,918 samples), sub-goal planning (4,187), and next tool call (9,771). For next-call samples, we convert each recorded action sequence into tool-call trajectory: gripper events and segment boundaries place the calls, and dataset annotations name the objects and spatial relations. Each step is rendered with the final harnesss observation and history format, so the student sees real scenes through the same interface it uses in simulation. The teacher then supplies the reasoning. It first predicts the call without seeing the reference; if the two match, its reasoning is kept. Otherwise, as in the rationalization step of STaR [51], it is given the reference call and asked to explain it, and the explanation is kept only if it passes consistency and quality checks. In both cases the dataset-derived call is the action target (details in Sec. F). 3.4. Student training and deployment Teacher data comes from training seeds of all 50 RoboTwin tasks, the 7 seen Guava tasks, and LIBERO-90 [26]; the final set has 83,753 decision samples, half of them simulated (composition and hyper-parameters in Sec. F). We fine-tune 5 all language-model parameters of Qwen3.5-4B [33] for 2 epochs; at deployment the student replaces the teacher inside the frozen harness, served in bf16 on one accelerator. 4. Experiments We first show how harness evolution improves frozen planners and how distillation transfers these gains to compact students. We then compare the final student with its teacher and other agents, and test its generalization to unseen benchmarks. Finally, we analyze training ingredients, recovery behavior, and inference compute cost. 4.1. Setup Benchmarks. We report six benchmarks. Three belong to benchmark families that supply training data: RoboTwin 2.0 [8] with all 50 tasks 10 evaluation seeds (500 episodes), Guava [27] with 15 tasks 30 official seeds (450 episodes; 7 tasks seen in training, 8 unseen), and LIBERO-PRO [58] with 300 episodes (three LIBERO [26] suites, original and four perturbation types, 2 seeds each). Three are never touched by RSI or training and test zero-shot transfer: SimplerEnv [23] (Visual Matching, 960 episodes on the Google Robot and WidowX), VLABench [55] (the first 500 episodes of the official list over five tracks), and EB-Manipulation [48] (228 episodes). RoboTwin is also the RSI development benchmark. Acceptance decisions use only selection seeds; evaluation seeds ( 100,000) are disjoint from selection and training seeds (Sec. 3.2). Guava evaluation seeds are disjoint from our Guava training seeds, and LIBERO-PRO training data comes only from LIBERO-90. strict report success Evaluation protocol. We (Sec. 3.1) on the three training benchmarks and each benchmarks official success measure on the zero-shot benchmarks (Tab. 2). VLABench stops at the official success event and EB-Manipulation latches success; neither defines final-state predicate after done. All rates use fixed denominators. Episodes with undetermined outcomes count as failures; upper bounds counting them as successes and ever success are reported in Tab. 5. Comparisons between systems we run are paired on identical (task, seed) episodes; published results are listed separately. We report success rates and paired differences in percentage points. Within our harness, all evaluated planners decode at temperature 0 and share perception and motion-planning services. Competitor implementations and benchmark-specific configurations are detailed in Sec. B.

The first three rows keep model weights fixed across harness versions. The student row uses separately trained model for each version (Sec. 4.2). 4.2. Harness evolution and transfer to compact students Experimental design. We evaluate four harness versions, H1, H7, H16, and , on the same 500 RoboTwin episodes (Tab. 1). The teacher, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and the untrained 4B planner keep their weights fixed across versions. For each version, we collect teacher trajectories under the same collection-budget constraints and independently train student from the same Qwen3.5-4B checkpoint on successful episodes, using the same training recipe (Sec. F). Each student runs in its corresponding harness. Harness evolution. With teacher weights fixed, success rises from 33.4% under H1 to 63.6% under (full lineage in Tab. 8). The gains also transfer to other planners: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash [9], which was not the planner used during harness evolution, improves by 30.6 pp without model-specific harness changes. The untrained 4B planner improves from 14.6% to 41.2%. All three improve across the four measured versions. Distilling evolution gains. We train separate 4B student for each harness version. Student success increases from 36.2% at H1 to 62.8% at , with each student scoring close to its corresponding teacher (Tab. 1). Thus, improvements to the teachers harness carry into the distilled students. Within the final harness , the distilled student also outperforms the untrained 4B model by 21.6 percentage points (62.8% vs. 41.2%), showing the additional benefit of distillation. 4.3. Performance and generalization Student versus teacher. TinyAstral-4B stays close to its teacher on all three training benchmarks: 62.8% vs. 63.6% on RoboTwin, 93.6% vs. 94.7% on Guava, and 78.3% vs. 80.0% on LIBERO-PRO (Tab. 2). In the same harness, it also improves over the untrained 4B model by 18.4 pp on Guava and 42.0 pp on LIBERO-PRO; counting all undetermined outcomes as successes raises the untrained models Comparison with other agents. On the same evaluation episodes, TinyAstral-4B outperforms the tested open agents, including Guava-4B, PyRUA-Lean-4B, and SenseNova-RoboRSI-27B (Tab. 2). It also exceeds systems using our teacher model, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, in other harnesses: 93.6% vs. 78.9% for the Guava harness, and 78.3% vs. 57.3% and 53.0% for MotorMind and PyRUALean on LIBERO-PRO. PyRUA-Lean-4B is trained and self-evaluated with per-step environment success signal; without this signal, which our protocol withholds, it often declares success prematurely. These results highlight the contribution of the evolved harness and distilled policy to the final systems performance. Competitor-specific execution and scoring protocols are detailed in Sec. B. Generalization to unseen benchmarks. TinyAstral-4B also generalizes to three benchmarks never used for RSI or training: SimplerEnv, VLABench, and EB-Manipulation. Its success rates are within 5.0 pp of its teacher and within 2.4 pp of the 552B DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, all using the same harness (Tab. 2). Compared with the untrained 4B model, distillation improves performance across all four evaluation settings, with gains of 10.0 pp on SimplerEnv Google VM and 13.6 pp on VLABench. Despite receiving no training on these benchmarks, the student also exceeds published results from π0-FAST [30] on both SimplerEnv robots and π0 [3] on VLABench, although these baselines were fine-tuned on in-domain data (protocol details in Sec. C). Smaller students. TinyAstral-0.8B reaches 61.8% on RoboTwin and 93.8% on Guava, close to the 4B student, but falls to 54.7% on LIBERO-PRO compared with 78.3%. On the zero-shot benchmarks, both the 0.8B and 2B students remain within 3.0 pp of the 4B model across all four settings. The effect of model size is therefore most pronounced on LIBERO-PRO among the evaluated benchmarks (Tab. 2). 4.4. Ablations and recovery behavior Teacher reasoning. Keeping the teachers reasoning has the largest measured effect among our ablations (Tab. 3). Removing the reasoning text while keeping all training samples otherwise unchanged lowers success by 19.3 pp on LIBERO-PRO, 11.2 pp on SimplerEnv Google VM, and 10.0 pp on VLABench. On LIBERO-PRO, 49 of 300 episodes end at the call limit without reasoning, compared with 7 under the full recipe. Auxiliary real-robot data raises next-call accuracy on held-out supervision. TinyAstral-4B recovers on its own (original evaluation runs, final harness ; blue labels: zero-shot). Top two rows: closed loop on real SO-ARM101 arm; middle two: training domains; bottom two: zero-shot. Cards: tool calls and returned codes verbatim from the logs; amber: the decisive step; bubbles: the students reasoning before it. More examples, including Guava and distilled-vs-untrained comparison on one episode, are in Figs. 4 and 5. In their deployed SimplerEnv episodes for each system. configurations, the student uses 25.3 accelerators against 123.8 for the teacher (4.9) and 249.6 for DeepSeek-V4.1Flash (9.9), and its median episode is also the shortest (25.3 vs. 31.0 and 31.2 s; Tab. 4). The 4B student is served in bf16 on one accelerator without quantization or speculative decoding; the teacher uses four accelerators with FP8 weights and tensor parallelism, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash uses eight. 5. Conclusion TinyAstral first improves frozen teacher through harness evolution, then distills its reasoning and recovery behavior into compact student deployed in the final harness. Across four harness versions, students trained from later versions perform better and stay close to their corresponding teachers, showing that harness improvements carry into compact agents. The harness gains also transfer to other frozen planners. The final 4B student outperforms every open competitor we ran on identical episodes, stays close to its teacher on three training benchmarks, scores close to 552B planner on unseen benchmarks, and uses about one fifth of the teachers accelerator time in our deployment measurement. These results support harness evolution followed by distillation as route to capable robot agents with lower inference compute cost. Future work will extend the approach to more RSI environments.

F. Training details The 41,877 simulated samples comprise 13,857 RoboTwin, 9,054 Guava, and 11,159 LIBERO main-episode samples, plus 3,471, 2,048, and 2,288 recovery-branch samples, respectively. Each sample is one decision, with the loss applied only to the final assistant turn. The vision encoder and projector stay frozen. Training uses learning rate 105 with cosine decay and 5% warm-up, global batch of 32, and maximum length of 12,288 tokens. Explanations given the reference call are rejected if they refer to the supplied answer, claim unmeasured success, omit the target object or required reference, or violate the length and format constraints. Next-call relabeling retained 19,598 of 23,070 candidate steps: 4,509 whose reasoning comes from matching first prediction and 15,089 explained given the reference call. The 9,771 next-call training samples are drawn from this pool. G. Harness interface details Observations. On RoboTwin, ot contains RGB images from the head camera and both wrist cameras, the task instruction together with the names of scene objects, proprioceptive line with the measured gripper state of each arm, the result rt1 of the previous call, and counter of calls used. Images are kept for the two most recent turns only. Earlier turns retain their text, and earlier assistant messages retain only the tool call, without reasoning. On RoboTwin the first turn also includes the task note (Sec. 3.2). Guava and LIBERO-PRO use the same planner loop and tool semantics through benchmark adapters, keeping the three most recent single-view images. Tools. The RoboTwin harness exposes object-level tools: locate, grasp (with an optional part such as handle, rim, or end), place and carry (relative to reference object, with optional facing or turning), handover, lift, articulate, press, push, pour, move, release, home, bimanual (two calls executed in parallel), verify, done, and give up. Tools report what they measured rather than what they intended. For example, place re-measures the object after release and returns OFF TARGET with the offset if the object missed its target. check whose value cannot be measured reliably is returned as unknown (ok=null) rather than as pass.
